analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier to win antitrust lawsuits against price-fixing that raises consumer prices.
analysis.headline: The bill passed the Senate 61-37 on cloture and passed the Senate by voice vote, then the House replaced its text with a similar House bill; the House rejected the final conference report 175-225, and the bill died without becoming law.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the evidentiary standards in federal antitrust law for price-fixing cases. It would have made it easier for a small business or consumer to win a lawsuit claiming a supplier and its competitors conspired to cut off a discounting reseller. It would also have made an agreement between a supplier and a reseller to set resale prices automatically illegal, a rule designed to keep discount stores able to undercut manufacturers' preferred prices. The bill passed the Senate after overcoming two cloture votes, but the House rejected the final compromise report 175-225 and the bill died.
analysis.who_benefits: Discount retailers, small businesses, and consumers, by making it easier to sue suppliers who cut off discounters or collude on resale prices, with the aim of keeping consumer prices lower.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would make it easier for a small business or consumer to win a lawsuit claiming a supplier and its competitors conspired to cut off a discounting reseller, by allowing a jury to infer price-fixing from evidence that a supplier received a competitor's complaint about the reseller's pricing and then cut the reseller off.
It would make any agreement between a supplier and a reseller to set a resale price automatically illegal, with the goal of protecting discounters who undercut higher manufacturer-preferred prices.

The bill includes defenses for small suppliers lacking market power and preserves the rule of reason for vertical territorial and location restrictions, an attempt to limit the scope to conduct most likely to harm competition.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers and brand-name suppliers that police resale prices, and larger firms facing a greater risk of antitrust liability, who would bear the cost of more lawsuits and potentially higher litigation expenses.

drawbacks.text: Critics of resale price maintenance laws argue that allowing suppliers to set resale floors can protect small retailers from free-riding on the service and expertise of larger discounters, and that treating all resale price agreements as per se illegal may harm competition in some circumstances.
The bill would apply a new legal standard to some civil actions already in progress, which critics of the bill argued was unfair to defendants in pending litigation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's main benefit is making it easier to punish price-fixing that raises consumer prices. Its main cost is the risk of more antitrust litigation against manufacturers, some of which may be meritorious and some not. The bill includes safeguards for small firms and vertical restraints, but the per se treatment of minimum resale price agreements remains the most contested part of the design.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed the bill, but the House passed a different version; after a conference committee filed a compromise report, the House rejected it on a 175-225 roll-call vote, and the bill died without becoming law.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate in February 1991 and referred to the Judiciary Committee, which held hearings and reported it to the Senate floor.
The Senate overcame two cloture votes, 61-37 and 63-35, before passing the bill by voice vote on May 9, 1991.

The House took up the Senate bill only as a vehicle to pass its own version, striking the Senate text and inserting the text of H.R. 1470, the Price Fixing Prevention Act of 1991, which passed without objection.
The two chambers' conferees agreed to file a compromise report in June 1992, but the House rejected the report on a 175-225 roll-call vote on June 30, 1992, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers and large suppliers opposed to tighter antitrust enforcement of resale pricing won, because the House rejected the compromise report and the bill died without becoming law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Manufacturers opposed to the tighter rules

for.name: Sen. Howard Metzenbaum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as a Senate conferee.

for.name: Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Supplied most of the votes to overcome cloture and pass the bill; 50 of 56 voting Democrats supported cloture.

for.name: House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Supplied 165 of 175 votes for the conference report, though 73 Democrats voted no.

for.name: Sen. Joseph Biden
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill to the Senate floor and served as a Senate conferee.

for.name: Rep. Jack Brooks
for.what_they_did: Served as a House conferee and brought the conference report to the House floor for a vote.

against.name: House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Supplied 152 of the 225 votes against the conference report.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted against cloture on the motion to proceed 32-11, forcing a 60-vote threshold before the bill could reach the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had strong bipartisan sponsorship in the Senate, with 31 cosponsors including 4 Republicans, but Senate Republicans largely opposed it, supplying 32 of 37 no votes on the first cloture vote, while House Republicans supplied 152 of 225 no votes on the conference report; 73 House Democrats also voted no.

industries.note: The bill would have exposed suppliers to a new legal risk when they cut off discounting resellers or set minimum resale prices, which would have made it harder to keep prices high through resale pricing policies.
The bill would have made it easier for discounters to sue suppliers who cut them off for pricing below manufacturers' preferred levels, supporting the discounters' ability to offer lower prices.
The new evidentiary standards would have changed the legal landscape for ongoing and future price-fixing litigation, benefiting some litigants and their counsel.
